source.title: Exploring Scaling Laws for Local SGD in Large Language Model Training
source.authors: Qiaozhi He; Xiaomin Zhuang; Zhi-Hua Wu

page_placements.theme: Architectural changes shift loss levels and efficiency frontiers

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether held-out validation loss follows parameter-count scaling under local SGD, using a different training setup from the original scaling-law studies and comparing with DDP.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-loss scaling fits against parameter count and a larger-model validation. It also reports local-update-step effects, communication-efficiency calculations, and multi-cluster scenarios; these do not measure the claim versions' named relationships. Foundational scaling-law results cited from other work are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own eight-model sweep (5M–800M non-embedding parameters) with local SGD and DDP. It fits validation loss against parameter count on SlimPajama and C4, then checks the fit against a 3B model. These are its own results on whether loss follows a parameter-count power law (V1) and whether small-run fits predict a larger run (V2).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that local SGD follows a parameter-count scaling law comparable to DDP, and that the fit predicts a 3B model. They also derive an analytical multi-cluster efficiency K and a combined L(K,N) law. From these they argue that local SGD can match DDP under adequate inter-cluster bandwidth (λ≈2e-3 for 8 clusters at 0.8 Gbps), and they set out the bandwidth limits for multi-cluster and edge training. These scenario results are calculations, not empirically validated.
record.recipe_differences: Uses local SGD with periodic synchronization and compares it with DDP, rather than reproducing the original studies' training setups. It uses validation cross-entropy loss and parameter-count fits; it does not test the original studies' compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that smaller local-update intervals cause less performance degradation, but does not report this as a sensitivity of the fitted parameter-count exponents. It uses AdamW as the inner optimizer and Nesterov momentum as the outer optimizer.

fits_no_version.finding: Local SGD with 32 local steps yields parameter-scaling exponents nearly identical to DDP (0.072 vs 0.069 on C4, 0.064 vs 0.063 on SlimPajama).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The parameter-count scaling exponent is insensitive to switching from synchronous DDP to low-communication local SGD at equal batch size and data.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss rises roughly linearly with the number of local update steps s, fitted as L(s,N)≈α_s·s+L(N) for s<1024 (Fig. 3, Eq. 3.6), for 0.1B and 0.8B models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Local-update interval adds an approximately linear loss penalty on top of the parameter-count power law.

record.problems: The parameter-scaling experiments cover eight models from 5 million to 800 million parameters and a validation model at 3 billion parameters. The paper does not give numerical prediction errors or uncertainty estimates for the scaling fits. It states that computational resources were limited and that its large multi-cluster scenarios lack empirical validation; those scenarios are not the parameter-count validation results recorded here.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant version-tested results were left out. Local-update-step plots and training-loss spikes (Figure 3), and K communication-efficiency calculations and plots (Sections 3.4.1–3.4.2 and Figure 4), do not measure the claim versions' specified loss relationships or allocation trend.

untested.parts: Loss versus training tokens or compute; parameter scaling beyond about 2 orders of magnitude; explicit confirmation that data was not the bottleneck (token counts not reported).
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude (only about 4x is tested); quantified prediction error; token- or compute-based extrapolation.
No variation of shape at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. Local SGD text pretraining does not fall under this version.

No comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting or schedules aimed at exponent dependence. Only small exponent differences across validation sets and optimizers are reported, and they are not analysed.

missing.what: Local-update-step effect on validation loss for 0.1B and 0.8B models and the fitted linear term α_s. This is the basis of the L(s,N) law; it is not a V1–V7 result but is a scaling-form result on loss.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V5 links are dropped: an optimizer change within text pretraining is not the beyond-text-pretraining regime that V5 names. The fitted form is a pure power law with no irreducible-loss term. Exponents (about 0.063–0.072) are close to Kaplan's 0.076. No uncertainties are reported. The Figure 1 exponent signs are lost in the text extraction. The multi-cluster K analyses (Fig. 4) are analytical throughput estimates, correctly excluded from rows.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss versus parameter count for models trained with local SGD and DDP. Does not test scaling versus training tokens or compute, or vary those quantities while holding the other factors non-bottleneck.

Reports validation of a fitted parameter-count curve on a 3-billion-parameter model. Does not report extrapolation across other model families, training-token or compute scales, or numerical prediction errors.
No fixed-compute search for a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
No controlled variation of architecture depth, width, or other architectural details at fixed parameter count.
Tests local SGD as a different training/optimization regime on text pretraining. Does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

Does not compare fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, datasets, or training schedules to test whether exponents or optimal allocations depend on setup; it does not test curve bending away from a single power law.
